sections.content: [Placeholder passage text about geoglyphs in England: most are located in a particular area (south/southern England); more in the shape of a horse than any other creature; the Uffington White Horse was recently dated — people were mistaken about its age; historians have NOT come to an agreement about the Long Man of Wilmington's origins; geoglyphs were created by removing turf to expose white chalk (not placing chalk on hillside); many are still visible (not no longer visible); shapes have been altered over time; Uffington White Horse fame is NOT due to its size. Location: 2.5 km from Uffington village, near Ridgeway (ancient road), near barrows/burial mounds. Dating: first mention in documents from 1070s; coins 100 BCE–1 BCE show similar horses; sediment analysis shows Late Bronze Age / Early Iron Age. Possible reasons: land ownership symbol, ancient ritual, goddess Epona (protection of horses and fertility/riders), Welsh goddess Rhiannon.]

sections.content: [Placeholder passage text about microbes (based on Ed Yong's book 'I Contain Multitudes'): microbes adapt to environment; we have more microbial cells than human cells; a discovery about microbes and disease. Yong argues we should be more tolerant of microbes; only a small number cause illness; relationship with microbes is one of partnership. Microbes aid digestion, remove poisons, produce vitamins, may reduce obesity. Problems: poor nutrition, overuse of antibiotics, excessive focus on cleanliness. Antibacterial home products may fail to have desired effect. Children should NOT avoid bacteria. Book has appropriate number of case studies; squid example may have limited appeal; dengue fever control has been surprisingly successful; microbes in hospital walls are still being researched (not yet done).]

sections.content: [Placeholder passage text about wisdom: a basic assumption about wisdom may be wrong; Grossmann researches wise reasoning. Wise decision-making can vary greatly from person to person. Grossmann claims wisdom level is different in different circumstances (not fixed). The fifth paragraph describes a recommended strategy (avoiding first-person perspective) to reason wisely. Four characteristics of wise reasoning: intellectual humility/modesty about extent of knowledge, taking into account other opinions/viewpoints, broad view of situations, awareness of likelihood of change in relationships. Better to regard scenarios with detachment/objectivity; avoiding first-person perspective → focus on fairness and other moral ideals. Experiments: job prospects (students could choose perspective); couples experiment (participants NOT aware it was about wise reasoning; relationship length had NO impact on results); in both experiments, detached viewpoint led to wiser decisions. Wisdom is NOT determined mainly by intelligence.]
